items.stem: (i) Name three techniques/devices used by human females to avoid pregnancy. Mention the side effects caused by each. (ii) What will happen if in a human female (a) fertilisation takes place, (b) an egg is not fertilised?
items.answer: (i) The three techniques/devices used by human females to avoid pregnancy are: (a) Cervical Cap and Diaphragm — Side effects: If not fitted properly, it can lead to sexually transmitted infections and can cause vaginal irritation. (b) Loop and Copper-T — Side effects: They can cause irritation of the uterus, excess menstrual bleeding, pain and risk of infection. (c) Tubectomy — Side effects: If not performed properly, it can cause infections and other problems. (ii) (a) If fertilisation takes place, it will stop menstruation in the female. (b) If an egg is not fertilised, the overgrown lining of the uterus breaks down and comes out along with the unfertilised egg through the vagina with blood and mucus.

items.stem: (i) Draw a diagram showing spore formation in Rhizopus and label the (a) reproductive and (b) non-reproductive parts. Why does Rhizopus not multiply on a dry slice of bread? (ii) Name and explain the process by which reproduction takes place in Hydra.
items.answer: (i) Diagram showing spore formation in Rhizopus: the erect hyphae bear knob-like sporangia at their tips — the sporangium (with the spores it holds) is the reproductive part, while the hyphae/mycelium are the non-reproductive parts. In Hydra, a bud develops as an outgrowth due to repeated cell division at one specific site. These buds develop into tiny individuals and, when fully mature, detach from the parent body and become new independent individuals.

items.stem: What is carpel? Write the function of its various parts.
items.answer: The flask-shaped organ in the centre of a flower is called the carpel. It is also called the female reproductive organ of the plant. It is made up of three parts — 1. Stigma, 2. Style, 3. Ovary. 1. Stigma is the top part of the carpel and is sticky, so it receives the pollen from the anther of the stamen. 2. Style connects the stigma to the ovary and acts as the passage for the growth of the pollen tube. 3. Ovary contains the female gametes of the plant and helps in reproduction; it is the site of fertilisation.

items.stem: List the advantages of sexual reproduction.
items.answer: Sexual reproduction has many advantages, for example: (i) There is always a possibility of diversity of characters in the offspring because the offspring is formed as a result of fusion of two gametes produced by two different individuals — the male and the female parents. (ii) There is every opportunity for new combinations of characters, i.e., variations. (iii) New variations are essential for evolution and the origin of new species.

items.stem: How does the process of budding differ from the process of spore formation?
items.answer: Budding is the process of asexual reproduction where a bud develops as an outgrowth of the body due to repeated cell division and grows into a tiny individual which can later separate from the parent body, e.g., Hydra. items.stem: The organisms formed by asexual reproduction are considered as clones. Why? State the advantage of sexual reproduction over asexual reproduction.
items.answer: Organisms produced by asexual reproduction contain exactly the same number of chromosomes and the same DNA sequence as the parent cell. Hence they have no variations from the parent and look alike — they are clones. Sexual reproduction results in the mixing of gametes of two individuals, hence variation occurs in the offspring, leading to evolution.

items.stem: Explain external and internal fertilisation.
items.answer: Fertilisation is the process of fusion of the haploid male and female sex cells, i.e., sperm and ovum, which results in the formation of a zygote. External fertilisation: when the fusion of male and female gametes takes place outside the body of the female, e.g., fishes and frogs. Internal fertilisation: when the fusion of male and female gametes takes place inside the body of the female, e.g., birds, reptiles and mammals including human beings.

items.stem: How is the amount of DNA maintained in each generation?
items.answer: In sexual reproduction, the amount of DNA is maintained in each generation by a specialised mode of cell division called meiosis, which produces specialised male and female germ cells called gametes which are haploid. One male and one female gamete fertilise to give rise to a diploid zygote which has the same chromosome number as the parent. This process maintains the chromosome number and the amount of DNA in each generation. In asexual reproduction, mitosis takes place and only a single parent is involved, so the number of chromosomes in the progeny remains constant.

items.stem: What are the functions of testis in the human male reproductive system? Why are these located outside the abdominal cavity? Who is responsible for bringing about changes in appearance seen in boys at the time of puberty?
items.answer: The functions of the testes are (i) to produce male sex cells called sperms and (ii) to produce the male sex hormone called testosterone. The testosterone hormone brings about the secondary sex changes seen in the appearance of boys at the time of puberty. The testes are outside the abdominal cavity of the body because sperm formation requires a lower temperature than the normal body temperature. Being outside the abdominal cavity, the temperature of the scrotum is about 3°C lower than the temperature inside the body. In this way the testis provides an optimum temperature for the formation of sperms.

items.stem: What is multiple fission? How does it occur in an organism? Explain briefly. Name one organism which exhibits this type of reproduction.
items.answer: Division of a single-celled organism such as the malarial parasite Plasmodium into many daughter cells simultaneously is termed multiple fission. During multiple fission, the organism secretes a protective covering, the cyst, around the cell. Inside the cyst, the nucleus divides several times to form a number of daughter nuclei. Each daughter nucleus gets surrounded with a bit of cytoplasm. Thus a large number of daughter individuals are formed. On the arrival of favourable conditions, the cyst ruptures and the single-celled daughter individuals are set free, which grow into complete organisms. Plasmodium exhibits multiple fission.

items.answer: Hyphae of Rhizopus produce tiny structures called sporangia. In these bulbs of sporangia, a number of spores are produced through mitotic cell division, which are covered by thick walls. On maturation, the sporangia burst and release the spores, which germinate into new mycelium in moist conditions.

items.stem: What is meant by pollination? List its two types. State any two agents which help in pollination.
items.answer: Pollination is the process of transfer of pollen grains from the anther of the stamen to the stigma of the pistil of the flower. Types of pollination: (i) self-pollination, (ii) cross-pollination. Agents that help in pollination: wind and animals.

items.stem: Write one main difference between asexual and sexual modes of reproduction. Which species is likely to have comparatively better chances of survival — the one reproducing asexually or the one reproducing sexually? Give reasons to justify your answer.
items.answer: Asexual reproduction involves only one parent and the offspring produced are clones, similar copies of their parent, whereas sexual reproduction involves two parents and the offspring produced are different from their parents. Offspring produced by sexual reproduction have better chances of survival. Sexual reproduction leads to variation because it leads to the formation of offspring by the combination of DNA from both parents, so the species will have better adaptability and a better survival rate.

items.stem: Explain the term 'Regeneration' as used in relation to reproduction of organisms. Describe briefly how regeneration is carried out in multicellular organisms like Hydra.
items.answer: Regeneration: it is the ability to give rise to a new organism when the individual is cut or broken up into many pieces. Hydra uses regenerative cells for reproduction in the process of budding. In Hydra, a bud develops as an outgrowth due to repeated cell division at one specific site. These buds develop into tiny individuals and, when fully mature, detach from the parent body and become new independent individuals.

items.stem: (a) Explain the terms (i) implantation, (ii) placenta. (b) What is the average duration of human pregnancy?
items.answer: (a) (i) The embedding of the embryo in the thick lining of the uterus is called implantation. (ii) After implantation, a disc-like special tissue develops between the uterus wall and the embryo, called the placenta. The exchange of nutrients, oxygen and waste products between the embryo and the mother takes place through the placenta. (b) The average duration of human pregnancy is about nine months and ten days (40 weeks).

items.stem: How do organisms, whether reproducing asexually or sexually, maintain a constant chromosome number through several generations? Explain with the help of a suitable example.
items.answer: In sexual reproduction, the amount of DNA is maintained in each generation by a specialised mode of cell division called meiosis, which produces specialised male and female germ cells called gametes which are haploid. One male and one female gamete fertilise to give rise to a diploid zygote which has the same chromosome number as the parent — e.g., in human beings the gametes carry 23 chromosomes each and the zygote again has 46. In asexual reproduction only mitosis takes place and a single parent is involved, so the chromosome number in the progeny stays the same as the parent's.

(b) More people prefer to use condoms because (i) it prevents sexually transmitted diseases (STDs), and (ii) it gives privacy to the user. items.stem: (a) What is variation? How is variation created in a population? How does the creation of variation in a species promote survival? (b) Explain how offspring and parents of organisms reproducing sexually have the same number of chromosomes.
items.answer: (a) The difference in the characters among individuals of a species is called variation. (i) A basic event in reproduction is the creation of a DNA copy. Cells use chemical reactions to build copies of their DNA. The DNA in the cell nucleus is the information source for making proteins. If the information is changed, different proteins will be made. Different proteins will eventually lead to altered body designs. This causes variations among the population. (ii) The great advantage of variation to a species is that it increases the chances of its survival in a changing environment. For example, the accumulation of heat-resistant variation in some bacteria will ensure their survival even when the temperature in the environment rises too much due to a heat wave; the bacteria which did not have the variation to withstand heat would not survive. (b) In sexual reproduction, organisms produce gametes through a special type of division, meiosis (reductional division), in which the original number of chromosomes becomes half. These two gametes then combine to form the zygote and the original number of chromosomes is restored, as in the case of human beings.

items.stem: (a) Draw a neat labelled diagram of a pistil showing germination of pollen on the stigma. (b) Give the functions of: (i) Stigma (ii) Ovary. (c) State in brief the formation of seed in a flower.
items.answer: (a) A labelled diagram of the pistil showing a pollen grain germinating on the stigma and the pollen tube growing down the style into the ovary to reach an ovule. (b) Function of stigma: the stigma is the site of pollination — the pollen grain lands on the stigma, which is generally sticky, and here it begins to germinate. Function of ovary: the ovary bears the ovules containing the female gametes and is the site of fertilisation; after fertilisation it ripens into the fruit. (c) After the pollen tube delivers the male gamete to the ovule, the male and female gametes fuse to form the zygote. The zygote divides to form the embryo inside the ovule, the ovule develops a tough coat and is converted into the seed, while the ovary ripens into the fruit.

items.stem: List six specific characteristics of sexual reproduction.
items.answer: Characteristics of sexual reproduction: (i) Two parents are involved. (ii) Two dissimilar gametes are formed and gamete formation involves meiosis. (iii) Variations are produced. (iv) It occurs in all the higher and some of the lower organisms. (v) Fertilisation of gametes leads to zygote formation. (vi) It is a slow process.

items.stem: (a) What is the difference between self-pollination and cross-pollination? (b) What happens to the pollen which falls on a suitable stigma? Explain.
items.answer: (a) Self-pollination is the transfer of pollen grains from the anther of one flower to the stigma of the same flower or another flower of the same plant. Cross-pollination is the transfer of pollen grains from the anther of one flower to the stigma of another flower growing on another plant of the same species. (b) Soon after pollination, the pollen grain starts germinating and forms a pollen tube. The pollen tube grows through the style until it reaches the embryo sac of the ovule, where it fertilises the female gamete.

items.stem: (i) What is vegetative propagation? (ii) What methods will you use for growing jasmine and rose plants?
items.answer: (i) It is a means of propagation in which new plants are obtained from the vegetative parts of old plants like stem, roots and leaves, without the help of any reproductive organ. Vegetative propagation is of two types: (a) natural and (b) artificial. (ii) The layering method of artificial vegetative propagation can be used for growing jasmine plants. The stem-cutting method of artificial vegetative propagation can be used for growing rose plants.

items.stem: (a) State any two changes seen in boys at the time of puberty. (b) Define fertilisation and implantation. (c) State the role of ovary and fallopian tube in the human body.
items.answer: (a) (i) Boys begin to have thick hair growth on the face. (ii) Their voices begin to crack. (b) Fertilisation is the fusion of haploid male and female gametes to form a diploid zygote. Implantation is the process of attachment of the embryo to the uterine wall for further development. (c) The fallopian tube is the site where fertilisation occurs. The ovary produces the female gamete and also secretes the female sex hormones estrogen and progesterone.

items.stem: (a) Write the functions of the following parts in the human female reproductive system: (i) Ovary, (ii) Oviduct, (iii) Uterus. (b) Write the structure and function of placenta.
items.answer: (a) (i) Ovary: production of ova and sex hormones. (ii) Oviduct: site of fertilisation. (iii) Uterus: keeps the foetus implanted till complete development. (b) Placenta: a special tissue embedded in the uterus wall with the help of which the human embryo gets nutrition from the mother's blood. Functions: (i) to provide a large surface area for glucose and O₂ to pass from the mother's blood to the embryo; (ii) the metabolic waste generated by the embryo is removed through the placenta into the mother's blood.

items.stem: Differentiate between (a) Plumule and radicle (b) Pollination and fertilisation.
items.answer: (a) The plumule becomes the shoot and the radicle becomes the root of the plant. (b) Pollination is the process of transfer of pollen grains from the anther of the stamen to the stigma of the pistil of the flower; its types are (i) self-pollination and (ii) cross-pollination, and the agents that help in pollination are wind and animals. Fertilisation is the fusion of the male and female gametes; its types are external fertilisation — when the fusion of male and female gametes takes place outside the body of the female, e.g., fishes and frogs — and internal fertilisation — when the fusion takes place inside the body of the female, e.g., birds, reptiles and mammals including human beings.

items.stem: Define pollination. Explain the different types of pollination. List two agents of pollination. How does suitable pollination lead to fertilisation?
items.answer: Pollination is the transfer of pollen from the anther of the stamen to the stigma of the pistil with the help of air, water and insects. Types of pollination: 1. Self-pollination — transfer of a pollen grain from the anther to the stigma of the same flower. 2. Cross-pollination — transfer of a pollen grain from the anther of one flower to the stigma of another flower of the same species. Two agents of pollination are air and insects (water and wind also act as agents). When the correct species of pollen grain lands on the stigma, it results in a chemical response from the ovary that causes the growth of a pollen tube from the pollen grain. The male gamete slides down the pollen tube and enters the ovary where it meets the egg. This process is called fertilisation and leads to the formation of the zygote.

items.stem: A student wants to germinate dicot seeds. Write the four steps in correct sequence that will help him to perform the experiment in the right way.
items.answer: Steps to perform the seed germination experiment are as follows: 1. Collect 10-15 whole and undamaged dicot seeds of gram, soybean or mungbean. 2. Now put these seeds in a beaker of fresh water, or first dip them into water for a few minutes and then put them into a wet cloth along with a wet cotton ball. 3. Now observe these seeds after 24-26 hours. 4. We will see a white-coloured thread-like radicle (future root) which starts to absorb water actively to initiate the development of the seedling. It is the result of seed germination.

items.stem: What are the aspects included in reproductive health?
items.answer: The aspects included in reproductive health are: (i) awareness regarding fertility regulation methods; (ii) the right, the freedom and the choice to control child birth; (iii) the ability to prevent and control sexually transmitted diseases; (iv) to manage disorders related to the reproductive system.

items.stem: (a) How will an organism be benefited if it reproduces through spores? (b) How is regeneration different from fragmentation?
items.answer: (a) Spores remain viable for a longer period because of the presence of a thick wall, even under adverse environmental conditions. (b) Regeneration involves the production of a complete new individual due to the ability of the parent organism to replace its lost body parts. Fragmentation is an asexual mode of reproduction in which a multicellular organism breaks up into smaller pieces upon maturation and these pieces result in the formation of complete new individuals. It may or may not involve differentiation.

items.stem: Write the two causes of human population explosion. Explain with the help of suitable examples how this explosion can be checked.
items.answer: Causes of human population explosion are (i) poverty and (ii) lack of family planning. Family planning enables a couple to decide on the number of children they want to have and when to have them. Family planning can be done by practising birth control measures. Birth control can be done by preventing pregnancy in females. Pregnancy can be prevented either by adopting a method or procedure by which the sperms produced during copulation can be prevented from meeting the ovum (or egg) and fertilising it, or by preventing implantation of the embryo. Since frequent pregnancies add to our already exploding population, a number of techniques or methods have been developed to prevent pregnancies in women.

items.stem: Answer the following questions: (a) What happens if an egg is not fertilised? (b) Why do we need to adopt contraceptive measures? Name one bacterial and one viral sexually transmitted disease.
items.answer: (a) If an egg is not fertilised then the entire endometrium or uterus lining is lost along with blood and tissues in the form of menstrual excretions. (b) (i) To prevent unwanted pregnancies. (ii) To prevent sexually transmitted diseases. (iii) For spacing between children. (iv) For sound health. Bacterial STD — gonorrhoea; viral STD — AIDS.
